This summary has been helpfully compiled with claude's assistance.

Lean4Lean: current state and how to help

Lean4Lean is a reimplementation of the Lean 4 kernel in Lean 4, together with a formalization of Lean's metatheory and an in-progress proof that the implementation satisfies the abstract specification — in the same general direction as MetaCoq, but for Lean. The executable checker has been done for a while: it checks Lean core and Mathlib, and the formalization effort has already found real kernel bugs. The interesting frontier now is the proofs, and there is a lot of well-scoped work available for anyone who wants to help push this to completion. This post is a map of what remains.

The repo has three layers:

  • Lean4Lean/*: the executable kernel, derived from the C++ implementation (deliberate differences are tracked in divergences.md).
  • Lean4Lean/Theory/*: the abstract metatheory — VExpr, VLevel, VEnv, the typing judgment and its properties.
  • Lean4Lean/Verify/*: the connection — proofs that the kernel functions are correct with respect to the Theory specification.

For the overall architecture see the paper Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean.

Axioms.lean: the trust base at the bottom

Verify/Axioms.lean is mostly not intended to be proved. It records our assumptions about the behavior of partial functions and C++-implemented functions at the lowest accessible level — things the Lean logic cannot see through. They come in a few flavors:

  • Opaque or partial upstream code. PersistentHashMap.insertAux and findAux, PersistentArray.push's insertNewLeaf, Syntax.structEq, mkAppRangeAux — these are partial or opaque, so nothing about them is provable; we axiomatize their observable behavior (e.g. insert behaves like insertion into an association list, up to permutation). Several have upstream issues attached (lean4#12798, lean4#8464): if these functions are made total or non-opaque upstream, the axioms turn into theorems and can be deleted.
  • C++-implemented Expr/Level primitives. instantiate, abstract, liftLooseBVars, lowerLooseBVars, hasLooseBVar, eqv, equal, replace, the BEq Level instance, … Each axiom states that the C++ function agrees with a reference implementation written out in Lean — morally an @[implemented_by] read in the other direction. These are the real trusted base of the verification: we verify the kernel algorithm assuming the expression primitives do what their Lean models say.
  • Bit-twiddling. mkData_eq/mkAppData_eq expose the bit-packed Expr.Data/Level.Data representation so that the cached-flag getters (hasFVar, hasLevelParam, looseBVarRange, …) can be related to their structural definitions.

One historical note: some of the cached-flag axioms were false for a while due to a data-corruption bug (lean4#8554) that this project uncovered; the fix has long since been merged upstream. Since Expr.data is a computed field, these axioms should now actually be provable by structural induction from mkData_eq/mkAppData_eq — a nice self-contained bit-twiddling project that would move them out of the axiom list entirely. More generally, this file illustrates what the axiom layer is for: it is where the interface between the formalization and reality is written down, and auditing it is itself useful work. Contributions here look like proofs like the above, upstream PRs that shrink the file (making functions total/non-opaque), and review that each remaining axiom faithfully models the C++ behavior.

The sorries

Outside of Experimental/ (which is a lab for work-in-progress ideas, where sorries are expected), there are about 22 sorries, and they are much more structured than the raw count suggests: one root accounts for most of them.

Root: the missing inductive type specification

Theory/Inductive.lean is seven lines long and contains the two most consequential sorries in the repo:

def VInductDecl.WF (env : VEnv) (decl : VInductDecl) : Prop := sorry
def VEnv.addInduct (env : VEnv) (decl : VInductDecl) : Option VEnv := sorry

That is: the abstract theory currently has no specification of inductive types at all. VInductDecl records the syntax of a mutual inductive block, but well-formedness (positivity, universe constraints, large elimination) and the effect of adding one to the environment (recursor types, iota rules) are unspecified. The specification also has to cover nested inductive types (which the kernel compiles away by a translation) and primitive projections / structure eta, neither of which the theory currently models — VExpr doesn't even have a projection former, so a .proj must translate to its recursor unfolding.

Nearly everything else that is sorried hangs off this one hole:

  • addInduct_WF (InductiveLemmas.lean): adding a well-formed inductive preserves environment orderedness. This feeds VEnv.WF → Ordered, a hypothesis of essentially every theorem in Theory/Typing and Verify/Typing.
  • The Params class in ChurchRosser.lean abstracts the non-beta reduction rules as patterns (left-hand sides that behave like constructor forms). No instance exists, because the iota rules that would instantiate it don't exist yet. The two sorries inside the Church–Rosser proof (the "extra rule commutes with congruence" cases of NormalEq.parRed) are part of the same obligation.
  • TrProj (Verify/Typing/Expr.lean), the translation relation for Expr.proj, is literally sorry as a definition, and the seven sorries in Verify/Typing/Lemmas.lean are the structural lemmas (weakening, substitution, congruence, uniqueness) that any real definition will owe. Similarly, AddInduct (Verify/Environment/Basic.lean) — the relation connecting the kernel's addInductive to the abstract VEnv.addInduct — is an inductive with no constructors, a sorry in disguise: as it stands, environments containing inductive types are outside the verified TrEnv relation.
  • In the verified typechecker, every remaining hole is an inductive-dependent rule: reduceRecursor.WF (iota, including quotient reduction), reduceProj.WF, inferProj.WF, tryEtaStructCore.WF (structure eta), isDefEqUnitLike.WF. Everything around them — inferType, whnf, isDefEq on the non-inductive fragment — is proved.

So "specify inductive types" is not one work item among many; it is the gate for the whole second half of the project. It is also largely design work before it is proof work, and a good fit for someone who enjoys type theory more than proof golf.

Injectivity.lean: the hard math

Theory/Typing/Injectivity.lean states three theorems, with the honest file docstring "A bunch of important structural theorems which we can't prove :(":

  • sort_inv: Sort u ≡ Sort v implies u ≈ v;
  • forallE_inv_stratified: injectivity of Pi under defeq (in a stratified form suitable for the well-founded induction that consumes it);
  • sort_forallE_inv: a sort is never defeq to a Pi.

These are the classical inversion/injectivity properties of definitional equality, and they are hard — the usual proofs go through normalization or a logical relation. They gate a lot: IsDefEq.uniq (unique typing) in UniqueTyping.lean is architecturally complete — a ~100-line well-founded induction — but rests squarely on these three sorries, and Church–Rosser and the whole Verify/TypeChecker stack consume unique typing.

This is where Experimental/ comes in. The current line of attack is a shape-indexed logical relation over a domain-model semantics (finite approximations of values in a Coquand–Huber-style domain, with the shape depth serving as the induction measure). The pipeline SExpr → Shape → Sound → LogRel → Adequacy gets remarkably far: the SExpr analogues of all three injectivity theorems are proved from the adequacy theorem, and Experimental/UniqueTyping.lean derives full unique typing from them without stratified judgments. Two things stand between this and discharging the sorries in Theory/:

  1. The const/rewrite-rule case of adequacy — the extension of the logical relation to environment constants and their unfolding rules. This is an open architectural problem, documented in detail in the code comments and in the LaTeX design notes (Experimental/logrel/main.tex). The constant-free core calculus is essentially done.
  2. The SExpr→VExpr merge — the experimental development uses its own expression type with explicit substitutions; porting the result back onto the main VExpr judgment is a substantial but well-understood refactor.

The same mathematics has also been developed in a standalone, cleaner setting: domain-semantics-lean is a self-contained Lean formalization of the domain model with soundness, adequacy, Pi/sort injectivity, and unique typing for an MLTT-style calculus, and there is a paper about the method, Definitional Inversion, Without Normalisation. If you want to understand the intended proof before diving into the lean4lean-specific version, start there.

There is one more independent sorry in this area: IsDefEqU.weakN_iff (UniqueTyping.lean) — the strengthening direction (defeq of weakened terms implies defeq of the originals). Only the forward direction is proved, and a family of weakN_iff/weak'_iff lemmas plus a few uses in Church–Rosser and the cache-typing invariants depend on it.

Missing theorems

Beyond the sorries, there are theorems whose statements don't exist in the repo yet. This is arguably the more important list, since a sorry at least records an obligation.

The front-end theorem and the environment layer

The strongest theorems currently proved are, roughly: relative to a context that assumes a well-formed environment translation (TrEnv), if checkType e returns ty then e and ty translate to a valid abstract typing judgment; similarly whnf.WF, isDefEq.WF, inferType.WF. The theorem the whole project is aimed at is now stated, as a sorry, in Verify/Environment.lean:

theorem addDecl.WF (wf : ves.WF env) (decl : Declaration) :
    (addDecl env decl).WF fun env' =>
      ∃ ves', ves'.WF env' ∧ ∀ safety, ves.venv safety ≤ ves'.venv safety

— adding a declaration to a well-formed environment, when the checker succeeds, produces a well-formed environment extending it. But none of the pieces of the proof exist yet; the gap is the whole environment layer:

  • Environment.lean (addAxiom, addDefinition, addTheorem, addOpaque, addMutual, addDecl) has no theorems about it at all. Nothing relates Lean.Kernel.Environment.add to the TrEnv constructors.
  • TrEnv is only ever consumed as a hypothesis; no theorem shows any of the add* functions produce it. Nobody ever constructs a VEnvs.WF.
  • The repackaging step — from "checkType succeeded in the empty local context" to the abstract VDefVal.WF premise that TrEnv extension needs — is missing.
  • The quotient layer is in the best shape (the abstract addQuot is specified and addQuot_WF is proved), but the link between the executable Environment.addQuot/checkEqType and the abstract AddQuot/QuotReady is still missing.

Much of this is straightforward-if-fiddly simulation-style proving, and it is largely independent of both the inductive spec and injectivity (one can state and prove the front-end theorem for the axiom/def/theorem fragment today). The main nontrivial input it needs is the HasPrimitives extension lemma described in the next section. Good entry point for someone who wants to contribute proofs without first absorbing the metatheory.

Primitives

Lean's kernel has special-cased reduction for Nat/String literals (GMP arithmetic for Nat.add and friends). Lean4Lean checks, at declaration time, that the primitives are declared with the right types and defining equations (Primitive.lean, ~500 lines of isDefEq checks — this is itself a divergence from the C++ kernel, which checks nothing and trusts the prelude). On the verification side, VEnv.HasPrimitives assumes exactly what is needed: e.g. that Nat.add applied to two literals is defeq to the literal sum.

There is currently no theorem connecting the two, and the front-end theorem is where the connection becomes unavoidable. Anyone who attempts addTheorem.WF or the like will find that re-establishing the environment invariant requires showing HasPrimitives is monotonic under environment extension — and it isn't, in full generality: the Reflects* fields are guarded by env.contains, so adding a constant named Nat.add activates new obligations that an arbitrary definition need not satisfy. Monotonicity holds exactly when the added declaration either is not a primitive, or is a primitive that computes on literals — and checkPrimitiveDef succeeding gives you precisely the facts (the checked defining equations, up to defeq) needed to prove the latter, by induction over the literals with the equations as rewrite steps (including the WellFounded.fix unfoldings for Nat.gcd and Nat.bitwise). So the missing piece is a HasPrimitives extension lemma, and it is a required stepping stone of the environment-layer work rather than an optional side quest. The same goes for the smaller safePrimitives assumption. The proofs themselves should be pleasantly concrete: verified evaluation of the recursive definitions of Nat.add, Nat.mul, ….

The level algorithm

Lean4Lean currently ships an experimental new algorithm for universe level normalization/comparison (normalize', isEquiv', geq'), which aims to be complete for level algebra. It has issues — there are known cases where it is incomplete relative to Lean's algorithm (e.g. max 2 v ≥ imax 2 v fails, which is reachable from the inductive constructor universe check), and its verification has a remaining sorry (NormLevel.subsumption_eval, correctness of the subsumption pass, which gates the top-level normalize_eval).

The plan of record is therefore to verify the original algorithm — the straightforward port of the C++ kernel's Level::geq — and keep the new algorithm as a backburner project (it is still interesting as a complete decision procedure, possibly in a hybrid arrangement later). Proving the original algorithm sound is a nicely self-contained task: pure syntactic reasoning about level expressions, no dependence on any of the rest.

Longer-term directions

Two further projects sit beyond the current scope of the repo but are very much part of the plan, and both could be started today by someone interested.

Soundness relative to ZFC + inaccessibles

Everything above is about the typechecker being faithful to the abstract typing judgment, plus structural properties of that judgment. None of it says the judgment itself is sound — that a well-formed environment cannot prove False. The plan here is to formalize the set-theoretic model construction from the final chapter of my masters thesis (The Type Theory of Lean): interpret Lean's type theory into a formalization of ZFC extended with countably many inaccessible cardinals (universes become inaccessibles, Prop becomes {0, 1} with proof irrelevance for free), giving consistency of the VEnv typing judgment relative to that base theory. This builds directly on the Theory/ layer — the interpretation function takes VExprs and typing derivations — and is largely independent of the verification work above. It does need its own infrastructure (a ZFC universe model; Mathlib's ZFSet and Cardinal.IsInaccessible are plausible starting points), and the paper proof has the usual subtleties around definitional equality soundness, but the target is written out in full detail in the thesis; "only" the formalization is missing.

Verified compilation

lean4lean deliberately does not support reduceNative (divergence #1), because trusting it amounts to trusting the whole compiler — verifying it "would be an additional chunk of work comparable to this entire repo". That chunk of work is this project: verify Lean's compiler, or some approximation of it, against the type theory. The model to follow is MetaCoq/MetaRocq's certified erasure — see Correct and Complete Type Checking and Certified Erasure for Coq, in Coq (Sozeau, Forster, Lennon-Bertrand, Tabareau, Winterhalter, JACM 2025) — which proves erasure from the dependently-typed calculus to the untyped λ□ ("lambda-box") intermediate language correct, and then feeds a growing family of verified backends. On the Lean side there is already motion: Bas Spitters' group has been working on connecting Lean to λ□ as part of the Peregrine Project (a unified λ□ middle-end for Agda, Lean, and Rocq, whose lbox tool emits OCaml via Malfunction, Wasm, Rust, C, and Elm; see also this 2025 report on compiling Lean programs via Rocq's extraction pipeline). What is missing is exactly the piece lean4lean's Theory/ layer is positioned to provide: a specification of Lean's erasure and a proof that it preserves the semantics of the typing judgment. Even a first cut — erasure for the non-unsafe fragment, proved correct against VEnv — would make native_decide and verified extraction for Lean far more trustworthy than they are today.

Summary: where to jump in

Roughly independent work packages, in increasing order of prerequisite knowledge:

  1. Level algorithm: verify the original C++ comparison algorithm. Self-contained, no metatheory needed.
  2. Primitives: the HasPrimitives extension lemma — checkPrimitiveDef succeeding implies the extended environment still HasPrimitives. Concrete computation proofs, and a prerequisite of the front-end theorem.
  3. Axioms.lean: prove the cached-flag axioms from mkData_eq now that lean4#8554 is fixed; upstream PRs to make functions total/non-opaque so axioms can be deleted; audit the remaining ones.
  4. Environment layer / front-end theorem: state and prove addDecl.WF for the non-inductive fragment. Simulation-style proving against the existing Verify/TypeChecker results.
  5. Inductive spec: design and write VInductDecl.WF and VEnv.addInduct, including nested inductives and primitive projections; then the TrProj lemma family and the five inductive-dependent typechecker theorems become available (and the Church–Rosser Params instance becomes constructible).
  6. Injectivity: the domain-model logical relation — either help finish the const case of adequacy and the SExpr→VExpr merge in Experimental/, or study the standalone domain-semantics-lean development and the accompanying paper.
  7. Set-theoretic model: formalize the ZFC + inaccessibles model of the Theory/ typing judgment, following the thesis. Independent of all of the above; needs set theory more than kernel internals.
  8. Verified compilation: specify Lean's erasure to λ□ and prove it correct against the type theory, MetaRocq-style, connecting to the existing λ□ backend ecosystem.

If any of these sounds appealing, say so here (or open an issue on the repo) and I can help you get oriented.

@Mario Carneiro, Codex and I started looking at proving HasPrimitives preservation. It seems problematic.

Quoth :robot::

I started investigating the HasPrimitives extension lemma and found what appears to be a verification obstruction in checkPrimitiveDef.

The open equations use:

let defeq1 a b := isDefEq (.arrow q(Nat) a) (.arrow q(Nat) b)

For example, the Nat.add check compares expressions equivalent to:

∀ _ : Nat, v.value #0 Nat.zero
∀ _ : Nat, #0

These are not well-typed Pi types: their bodies are Nat-valued terms, not types. Operationally this apparently uses forallE simply as a binder so that isDefEq compares the open bodies.

The existing verification theorem

isDefEq.WF
  (he₁ : c.TrExprS e₁ e₁')
  (he₂ : c.TrExprS e₂ e₂')

cannot be applied to these calls. TrExprS.forallE requires an IsType proof for the translated body, which is impossible here because the body has type Nat (or Bool) rather than a sort. Thus I cannot obtain the checked defining equation as an IsDefEqU fact. This occurs before any question of Pi injectivity: I cannot establish the premises of isDefEq.WF in the first place. (Nat.land and Nat.lor additionally use this Nat binder for an expression whose variable is intended to be Bool.)

There is a second compositional issue: in addDefinition, checkPrimitiveDef v runs before checkConstantVal and before checkType v.value. Therefore, at the point where its isDefEq calls run, the verification also has no TrExprS/typing facts for v.type or v.value.

So, more precisely, the executable bridge theorem “successful checkPrimitiveDef produces the defining-equation certificate needed to preserve HasPrimitives” does not seem provable through the current M.WF/isDefEq.WF interface. It might instead require a new specification for equality checking on raw open expressions.

Do you have a plan for this fake forall encoding?

For the proof, should we:

  1. preserve it and develop an appropriate open/raw-expression verification interface;
  2. change the checks to compare well-typed lambdas or use local declarations, and possibly run checkPrimitiveDef after the declaration has been type-checked; or
  3. some other route you have in mind?

I'm happy to announce that one of the big items from the list is now complete: Both level algorithms are fully verified.

  • The original level algorithm is sound: u ≈ v → isEquiv u v
  • The new level algorithm is sound: u ≈ v → isEquiv' u v
  • The new level algorithm is complete: isEquiv' u v → u ≈ v

The proofs follow the paper closely, but they include the new second part of the algorithm which converts sublevels back into levels for a proper normalization - normalize' u = normalize' v ↔ u ≈ v holds in general.
